headline: College Students Create Affordable Housing for Unhoused Peers
meta_description: Young adults across the U.S. are establishing and running low-cost shelters for classmates facing housing insecurity, offering both shelter and peer support.
summary_short: College students are building affordable housing solutions for peers struggling with homelessness, creating safe spaces where shared experience builds community.
body:
When Liam's family situation fell apart during his first year at UC Davis, he had nowhere to go. With little money and no support, he moved between temporary shelters until finding Aggie House, a collection of low-cost apartments run entirely by UC Davis students for classmates facing housing insecurity. There, he spent nine months living alongside other young adults navigating similar struggles—paying just $200 to $300 monthly in rent, roughly 90 percent less than the average cost of housing in Davis. What made the difference wasn't just the affordability: it was belonging to a community of peers who understood what it meant to be a student without a home.

Across the country, young adults are establishing similar housing initiatives. Y2Y shelter, founded by two Harvard students in 2015, operates from a basement near Harvard Square, housing up to 30 people between ages 18 and 24 from October through April. Unlike traditional emergency shelters, these peer-run spaces address a critical gap: young people often avoid adult shelters due to safety concerns or past trauma. About 3.5 million Americans between 18 and 25 experience homelessness annually, making them vulnerable to trafficking, violence, and worse.

What makes these initiatives powerful isn't just the beds or the low rent. At Aggie House, undergraduate volunteers prepare meals together, chat with residents about pop culture and school, and intentionally build social connection. As Hayven Angelique Pfister, a UC Davis student and external co-president of Aggie House, explains: when everyone shares the student experience, "it's easier and more comfortable" for people to open up about their struggles. These spaces recognize that homelessness among young adults often stems from family conflict, rejection, or aging out of foster care—challenges that peers understand intuitively. By stepping up for one another, these young adults are not just solving an immediate housing crisis; they're creating communities of healing.
quick_facts: UC Davis students created Aggie House in 2021 for housing-insecure peers
Residents pay $200–$300/month—90% less than average Davis rent
Y2Y shelter near Harvard Square houses 18–24-year-olds October through April
About 3.5 million Americans aged 18–25 experience homelessness annually
Peer-run shelters prioritize safety for LGBTQ+ youth and foster care alumni
